newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists elect new party leader.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists elect new party leader.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists on Tuesday elected Georgi Parvanov as party leader to replace Zhan Videnov who resigned on Saturday.
Parvanov told Reuters it had not been decided yet whether Videnov would stay on as prime minister. "This has yet to be debated," he said.
Videnov told reporters he did not rule out staying on as prime minister. "Such a solution is not excluded," he said.
Delegates to the marathon three-day party congress said Parvanov, a senior party official, was a compromise choice in the row between reformers and hardliners.
"Parvanov is a compromise figure between conflicting factions...being a more moderate person," said congress delegate and political analyst Miroslav Popov.
Parvanov, a member of the party's executive bureau, said a new cabinet would be appointed by mid-January.
"This is a sign of the commitment of the Socialist party to reform," Parvanov told the congress after his election.

Parvanov, 39, defeated reformist candidate Georgi Pirinski, the former foreign minister who resigned last month saying the government did not have the support it needed to carry out tough economic reforms.
Parliament will hold an extraordinary session on December 28 to vote on the resignation of Videnov's cabinet.

The showdown between party reformers and hardliners will delay government activity at a time when the 1997 budget is not yet finalised and the central bank is preparing to set up a currency board fixed exchange rate regime.
Parvanov said the new cabinet should include "strong figures" like Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, who led the attack on Videnov's record on Sunday.
Dobrev had been seen as a possible candidate as premier and party leader but delegates said he had declined to take the post.
The congress heard strong condemnation of the government's failure to halt economic collapse and curb corruption.
The Bulgarian lev has fallen steadily since the beginning of the year and sharply in the past two months as Bulgarians withdrew their savings from illiquid banks to convert them to dollars.

The International Monetary Fund and World Bank have suspended funding over Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets including closing or restructuring loss-making state enterprises and privatising viable firms.
